exam: A 35‑year‑old man with community‑acquired pneumonia is started on a macrolide. He develops tinnitus. — Identify the drug class, explain the adverse effect mechanism, and suggest monitoring strategy.
A 28‑year‑old HIV patient on zidovudine develops neutropenia. The clinician considers switching to a protein‑synthesis inhibitor. — Discuss the rationale, potential benefits, and risks of switching.

A 5‑year‑old child presents with fever and rash after a recent viral infection. The clinician suspects a bacterial superinfection and prescribes an aminoglycoside. — Explain why this choice may be inappropriate and propose an alternative.
A patient with severe sepsis is started on a protein‑synthesis inhibitor but shows no improvement after 48 h. The lab shows a high MIC. — Interpret the result and recommend next steps.

A 22‑year‑old student develops flu‑like symptoms after starting a viral protein‑synthesis inhibitor. — Differentiate drug‑induced symptoms from viral relapse and outline management.
ai.title: Block Protein Synthesis
ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: Antimicrobials that inhibit bacterial or viral protein synthesis act by targeting ribosomal subunits or associated factors, halting translation and leading to cell death or viral replication arrest. Clinically, choice depends on spectrum, resistance, and host factors.

sections.p: Block protein synthesis is a common antimicrobial strategy that stops the production of essential proteins in bacteria or viruses, leading to cell death or inhibition of viral replication. The mechanism targets ribosomal subunits or associated initiation factors.

Bacteria with 70S ribosomes (30S and 50S) are susceptible to antibiotics that bind these subunits. Viruses rely on host ribosomes; drugs that modify host initiation factors or activate antiviral pathways can block viral protein synthesis.
In bacterial infections, transmission is via direct contact, droplets, or contaminated surfaces. Viral infections spread similarly; the virus hijacks host ribosomes after entry and replication.
Inhibitors are used against a range of infections: bacterial pneumonia, meningitis, urinary tract infections, and viral diseases like influenza and HIV.
Diagnosis relies on clinical assessment and microbiological confirmation. For bacterial infections, culture and sensitivity guide therapy. Viral infections use PCR or antigen tests.

sections.p: Remember that protein synthesis inhibitors can cause ototoxicity (aminoglycosides) and myelosuppression (tetracyclines in children). Viral inhibitors often target host pathways, leading to side effects like flu‑like symptoms.

sections.p: Protein synthesis inhibitors are distinct from cell wall inhibitors (e.g., beta‑lactams) and DNA gyrase inhibitors (fluoroquinolones).
